read_from: The route text as served: field 1 (the route text) of each row of reader/data/route-store of the main branch at commit 306f3b285898, store_version 87b13b1169b4 (its index.json), for "Wikidata Hebrew source-explicit form linked to exact English lexeme sense" (M28, M10, M53, M48, M138): 11,440 routes (axis: routes), 10,488 letters keys (axis: keys), 1,703 distinct route texts (axis: texts). The definition field of the same row equals the route text on 11,440 of the routes, and the store's cut flag stands on 0. The source audit: each route's store record names a line of the lane's copy of the source (hebrew-explicit-forms-english-glosses.jsonl, in ledgers/work/ldmprs/source-cache/wikidata-hebrew-lexemes-2026-07-14/, one answer of Wikidata's query service) with its form and sense ids. The route text is the English text of that sense, the field skos:definition, on 11,440 of 11,440 routes (13 of them once a doubled space in the source is folded to one), and every one of the 2,037 senses of that file has one English text. So a route comes from one field, the text of one sense, and no test here stands on a guess about a field; the audit is evidence about the source and no part of any test. The source's own key to its signs: none found. The lane holds 9 files of this source that are no answers (the queries, the manifests, the licence page, in that folder); the only words in them that name a sign stand in 2 of the lane's own manifests and speak of the spelling of the Hebrew form, not of the English. Of the 5 files of the lane's work on the works' own stamps that name Wikidata, none is Wikidata's own account of how a sense's text is written, as the script builder/05-key-search.mjs and its output source-audit/key-search.json show. A manifest names Wikidata's documentation of its query service by its address (https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Wikidata:Lexicographical_data/Documentation/Query_Service); its body is not on file, and fetching it needs the owner's word. So every shape's meaning here begins "unverified:". What a sign does is read from the texts, and for the comma after a head word from the audit: 1,188 of the 1,770 senses behind the routes name an item of Wikidata, and the English label and description of that item stand in hebrew-explicit-forms-sense-item-english-fields.jsonl in the same folder.

definitions.terms: In every test a character is one Unicode code point (every route holds only characters of 16 bits, so a code point is one index of the JavaScript string). A letter is any character of Unicode category L (JavaScript \p{L}), of any script and in either case. A digit is one of 0 to 9, and no test asks for any other number character. A space is the character U+0020 only, and no test uses whitespace of any other kind. By name, a comma is «,», a semicolon is «;», a colon is «:», a slash is «/», an opening round bracket is «(», and a straight double quote is the character U+0022. Nothing is trimmed: the text is the whole route text as it stands, which is the field route of a line of the by-source JSONL, what the checker gives the classifier, and never the field def; the text before and the text after the mark are the template's c.before and c.after, and what a bracket holds is the template's c.group, the same for an opener and for its closer. Inside round brackets means that the template's c.container is the word paren. Directly before and directly after name the one character next to the mark or next to the named string; where the mark or the string stands at that end of the text no character stands there, so a test that asks for a character there fails, and a test that says no such character stands there holds. The whole text, exactly, means that the text equals the named string character for character. Begins with means that the first characters of the named thing are exactly the string, whatever follows them; it asks for no word end, and a space at the end of a string is part of the string. Ends with means the same for the last characters. Holds means that the string stands somewhere in the named thing as a run of characters, whatever stands beside it; it asks for no word end. A string stands between « and », which are not part of it, and a full stop or comma after » belongs to the sentence and not to the string. Every string and every list minds case and is matched exact to the character.
definitions.first_match: For each mark the shapes are tried in the order they stand in this file; the first whose test holds names the occurrence, and no later shape is tried for it. Not caught above means that no earlier shape of the same mark took the occurrence. A shape's container field is not part of its test: a test looks at the container only where it says inside round brackets, and the checker compares the field afterwards.
definitions.pair_steps: These steps are the same for an opener and for its closer. The text before the pair: for an opener, the text before the mark; for a closer, the text before the mark with its last characters taken off, as many as what the bracket holds has, and one more for the opener. The text after the pair: for an opener, the text after the mark with its first characters taken off, as many as what the bracket holds has, and one more for the closer; for a closer, the text after the mark.

homonyms.reason: The route text carries no entry number. The source gives each word (lexeme) an id, each sense of it an id and each written form of it an id (L18, L18-S1, L18-F1); the route store carries none of them, and the dictionary store's record keeps them in its location field. So two texts under one letters key may be two senses of one word or senses of two words, and the route text cannot say which. A letters key here is a written form of a word, inflected forms included, so a key counts forms and not headwords. By the audit, of the 814 keys with more than one text (axis: keys; 10,488 letters keys in all), 179 are keys whose routes all come from one lexeme, and 635 are keys whose routes come from two or more lexemes, words that share these letters (example key תקנו, whose 4 texts come from 4 lexemes).

branches.question: Here the source gives each sense of a word one text, and some texts hold several words for that sense, with a comma, a slash or a semicolon between them: big/large; alive, living; nation, ethnic group. No sign in the row can tell whether one of the words means something different from the rest, and the line between a second word and a short description is a judgment, made row by row: Anas, genus of birds is not in this question. Today the page cuts at those commas, and it does not cut at the slashes or the semicolons. Should these signs cut the row? From the day this is wired, these rows print whole, at the commas too. This answer holds whatever you answer to the other questions.

options.means: Every one of these signs in these rows cuts: the page prints big and large as two readings, and alive and living as two, each word as the source writes it. In a row that also holds a semicolon between two descriptions only the comma cuts: stone, rock; building material prints stone and rock; building material, and if you also rule that such a semicolon cuts, it prints stone and rock and building material.
No sign in these rows cuts: the page prints big/large and alive, living as one reading each, as written. At the commas this is a change from today.

branches.question: Some rows open with to and hold two or more words for one sense with a slash between them, where only the first has its to: to surround/encircle. No sign in the row can tell whether one of them means something different from the rest. Today the page does not cut at these slashes. Should the slash cut the row? Until you rule the page prints each of these rows whole. This answer holds whatever you answer to the other questions.

options.means: Every slash in these rows cuts: the page prints to surround and encircle as two readings. A later word prints as the source writes it, without the to; in to appear/be discovered the page prints to appear and be discovered, which keeps its own be.
No slash in these rows cuts: the page prints to surround/encircle as one reading, as written, as it does today.

branches.question: Some rows hold words with a slash between them that share a word written only once. In to be beaten/hit/struck the words hit and struck mean be hit and be struck; in evil/depraved person the word evil means evil person. Alone, such a word says something else. Should the slash cut the row? Until you rule the page prints each of these rows whole, as it does today. This answer holds whatever you answer to the other questions.

options.means: Every slash in these rows cuts: the page prints to be beaten, hit and struck as three readings, and evil and depraved person as two. Each piece prints as the source writes it, without the word it shares, so hit stands alone where the source means to be hit.
No slash in these rows cuts: the page prints to be beaten/hit/struck and evil/depraved person as one reading each, as written, as it does today.

branches.question: Some rows hold two or more words for one sense beside a note in round brackets, after a description or before a long tail: to provide/imbue (with something); Citrus medica, species of plant, citron. The note or the tail may speak of all the words. Should the slash in such a row, or the commas marked by hand in the rows that have them, cut the row? Today the page cuts at those commas and not at the slashes; from the day this is wired, each of these rows prints whole. This answer holds whatever you answer to the other questions.

options.means: The slash or the marked comma cuts, and a note or a tail stays where it stands, with the piece beside it, even when it speaks of all of them: the page prints to provide and imbue (with something) as two readings, and Citrus medica, species of plant and citron as two. A later word prints without the to or to be it shares, and with an or the source writes before it: in to be imbued/provided (with something) the piece provided (with something) stands alone where the source means to be provided, whatever you answer on to be beaten/hit/struck. A slash inside the brackets never cuts.
Nothing in these rows cuts: the page prints to provide/imbue (with something) and Citrus medica, species of plant, citron as one reading each, as written.

branches.question: Some rows hold two or more descriptions of the word, with a semicolon between them or, in some rows, a comma: son, male offspring; a boy or man in relation to his parents. The word at the head stands only before the first. Is each later description a further reading? Today the page cuts at those commas and not at the semicolons; from the day this is wired, each of these rows prints without a cut there. This answer holds whatever you answer to the other questions.

options.means: Every semicolon in these rows cuts, except one before a remark that opens with the word specifically, and so does the one comma marked by hand in the rows that have one: the page prints son, male offspring and a boy or man in relation to his parents as two readings. A later description prints without the word at the head, and with an or the source writes before it. The comma after son stays unless you also rule that such a comma cuts, in the question on several words for one sense.
No sign in these rows cuts there: the page prints son, male offspring; a boy or man in relation to his parents as one reading, as written.

branches.question: Some rows hold only a note on the word, or only a description of a person or a place, and no word that could stand in a verse: (indicates a semantically definite direct object); Biblical name; son of Nahor by Milcah. Should the page print them as readings? They print as written until you rule. To leave them out the page needs one step of its own, because a declaration cannot leave a row out. This answer holds whatever you answer to the other questions.

options.means: The page prints each row as one reading, as written: (expression of disbelief).
The page prints no pill for these rows, once it has the one step of its own that this answer needs; until then they print as written. They stay in the store as they are.
